However, this model has been disputed due to discrepancies between its discrete-time formulation and actual performance metrics. We investigate these discrepancies by scrutinizing the model's terms in discrete-time, revealing these terms' impact on link capacity. The results show link capacity is influenced by a unique combination of signal and delay channel noises, which can exceed the standard Gaussian noise in both cases. A new, modified link capacity formula is developed based on these findings, demonstrating its potential to limit link capacity in discrete-time conditions where the standard model falls short. We further explore how this modified formula applies to continuous-time scenarios, including cases involving multiband and single-band frequency-hopping channels. The analysis indicates these channels' capacity can be expressed as the minimum of individual frequency-band capacity formulas. We also assess a variant of the standard model involving amplified links, revealing its discrete-time formulation is analogous to its continuous-time version, which implies the variant is consistent in both cases. A comparison of average and outage link capacity metrics in discrete and continuous time reveals significant performance disparities, especially in discrete-time scenarios with non-Gaussian noise. We propose a new, simplified metric, the standard model error (SME), to quantify these performance disparities. A simulation involving various channel types and link lengths shows the SME can cause substantial capacity losses, which can be mitigated by adopting a modified link capacity formula and reduced SME strategies. These strategies include using noise-resilient coding techniques, such as repetition coding, and minimizing the standard model error. By scrutinizing the standard model's terms in discrete-time, we have gained valuable insights into their implications and developed a framework for improving link capacity and reducing SME in both discrete and continuous time scenarios. These improvements can be applied directly in discrete-time conditions, while continuous-time generalizations require additional steps to account for Gaussian noise in both the signal and delay channels. We have successfully bridged this gap by identifying the conditions under which discrete-time formulas can produce reliable results in continuous-time environments. Consequently, our work has provided a more precise understanding of the standard model's terms and a clear direction for enhancing link performance in both discrete and continuous time domains. The potential for capacity enhancements in discrete-time scenarios is substantial, while continuous-time generalizations may yield more modest gains, which still warrant further exploration. Predicting the future movements of numerous individuals in a crowded environment poses a particularly challenging task due to the dynamic nature of the data and the constant emergence of new interactions. In this context, the goal is to develop a predictive model that not only accounts for past behavior but also strives to minimize unexpected predictions. To tackle this issue, a novel method is introduced that reexamines prediction accuracy in a socially responsible light, emphasizing adherence to personal space while minimizing collisions. A model is proposed to dynamically update and predict comfortable personal spaces based on established safety principles. In conjunction, a predictive model is introduced that takes into account social responsibility, characterized by a computationally efficient variational graph neural network that learns and predicts safe and respectful interactions. To evaluate these methods, a new dataset is created by integrating social safety criteria into the standard OSM dataset used for trajectory prediction, demonstrating improved trajectory prediction accuracy and adherence to personal space while reducing collision risk. When applied to public crowds in real-world settings, the results show that socially-aware predictions are often preferred over solely predictive models. The code for these methods is available on the GitHub platform.

This paper examines various measures of network complexity using information theory and statistical mechanics as a basis. Specifically, our analysis on random Boltzmann networks reveals that certain non-parametric metrics are equivalent, while others yield distinct results. Furthermore, our comparison highlights a crucial trade-off between capturing network characteristics and loss of information associated with entropy-based measures. We discuss the practical implications of this equivalence and its potential applications in studying intricate systems by analyzing a corpus of internet topologies, demonstrating how certain details are missed in thermodynamic analyses but revealed by information-theoretic measures. We also demonstrate that information-theoretic measures can capture subtle patterns not visible in other metric systems, such as a decline in network complexity as the number of connections increases from zero. Finally, our analysis on a corpus of internet topologies indicates that meaningful insights can be gained from thermodynamic and information-theoretic measures, but detailed information-theoretic analysis is required to grasp the intricate properties of intricate systems. This study proposes a novel approach that integrates hand gesture recognition via a long short-term memory network to enable swarm robots to interact with their human environment. To capture distinct hand movements, on-board cameras on each robot record video sequences of a person's hand positions and orientations. A central processing unit analyzes these local video feeds, using a long short-term memory network to detect specific hand gestures. When a known gesture is detected, the processing unit sends a corresponding command signal to the relevant robot, which then synchronizes its motion with its fellow swarm members. In a subsequent step, the swarm collectively encircles and lifts a target object, exemplifying a practical application for this technology. A long-term evolution assessment, along with a convolutional neural network, has been successfully applied to this problem, showcasing its potential for real-world implementation on swarm robots. Video documentation of this system can be accessed at https://youtu.be/4h4g1uYk3gI. A GitHub repository containing the relevant code can be accessed at https://github.com/andreaspfister/handGestureLSTM. A separate repository containing the evaluation data can be accessed at https://github.com/andreaspfister/handGestureEval.

To address these challenges, our research focuses on the identification of rare white blood cells, specifically B cells, T cells, and monocytes, using a combined method of neural networks. By merging the outcomes of individual network models with unique training data, our ensembling method demonstrates superior performance and accuracy, outperforming existing single models. The findings of our study were verified through experiments using multiple common network architectures, as well as real-world images of human bone marrow marrows, making our results highly transferable to other similar tasks and applications. Overall, our research shows that ensembling is an effective technique for improving the accuracy and reliability of neural network models, especially in the complex field of digital pathology. Moreover, our results suggest that neural network ensembling can be a feasible and efficient method for real-world implementation, even on systems with limited resources and capacity. The combination of these results and insights has significant implications for the development of accurate and reliable AI tools in the field of digital pathology. The code and data used in this study are available on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/alexk99/BloodCellCat. The resulting models can be accessed through our Inference API at https://api.infershift.com. We present pyStoNED, a freely available, open-source Python library based on StoNED, a widely recognized method for measuring performance using single and multi-objective scenarios.  StoNED is a flexible, non-parametric approach that's easy to use and provides a straightforward analysis.  In this context, we'll be focusing on the non-decreasing version of StoNED, or StoNED-ND, as the negative outcomes aren't applicable in many real-world situations.  Our paper offers an accessible overview of the technique, as well as a comprehensive analysis of how to create it, providing an open-source alternative to other popular libraries such as Python's PESTO.  To support the non-parametric approach, we'll be using a complex dataset based on the sales of a new video game, as well as a multi-objective dataset based on the returns from different investment strategies.  To create pyStoNED, we've used a combination of the Django web framework and the crux library, designed for efficient, high-performance scientific computing in Python.  Ultimately, our new library is intended to make it easier to perform complex data analysis, either with or without a clear, defined objective. Inverse text standardization aims to normalize diverse representations of a single text into a unified form. This process has practical applications in processing varied text inputs, such as extracting keywords from social media or identifying text across multiple languages. Advanced neural models can achieve standardized output from a single encoder with this method. Nonetheless, existing inverse standardization techniques are limited by their inability to effectively handle out-of-vocabulary words and insufficient data for training, which impedes their ability to produce high-quality standardized output from encoders. This study presents a novel inverse standardization approach that leverages data augmentation to enhance performance and overcome these limitations. Experiments on various languages demonstrate the superiority of our proposed technique over existing methods. Furthermore, our results indicate that existing neural models can produce improved results when fine-tuned with our generated augmented data. This reveals the potential of augmented data to significantly enhance the performance of language processing tasks. Moreover, our proposed technique can also be applied to other neural language processing tasks. The paper also includes an in-depth analysis of the factors influencing the effectiveness of augmented data in linguistic processing tasks. Finally, we release our code and augmented corpus for public use. Additional details on our findings are documented in a companion paper. We establish the Faber-Krahn inequality for the first eigenvalue of the Hermite operator when subject to Robin boundary conditions, demonstrating its optimality when the parameter $\beta$ is non-negative and expressing its optimality otherwise in terms of a truncated infinite trapezoid. Furthermore, we determine the extremal domains for both scenarios. Moreover, we examine the case where the domain is symmetric about its center when subject to Robin boundary conditions, demonstrating optimality when $\beta$ is non-negative and deriving the optimality conditions otherwise. Furthermore, we investigate the optimality of the tangential Faber-Krahn inequality for the same scenarios. Our findings involve both functional inequalities and geometric properties of the extremal domains, expressed both in absolute and relative terms. The results are derived using a combination of isoperimetric inequalities, radial minimization, and geometric analysis. The analysis is complemented by an investigation of the domains that realize the equality in the inequality, with a focus on their structural properties, including their support, convexity, and features at the origin, as well as their area and perimeter when subject to Robin boundary conditions. The analysis reveals interesting results, including the possibility of having no support at the origin and a zero measure set that contains the point (0,0), and other limiting cases depending on the value of $\beta$. The findings can be summarized as follows. When $\beta$ is non-negative, the optimality is achieved by balls. Human intestinal parasitic infections, caused by a multitude of species, are a significant global health concern, linked to severe social and economic problems. However, the limited number of intestinal parasitic species, combined with their distinct morphological differences, presents an manageable categorization challenge in comparison to other medical issues. This paper presents a comprehensive overview of a system designed to automate the categorization of intestinal parasites through analysis of a dataset featuring digitized images of specimens from various institutions. Utilizing a dataset of 27,445 images from 13 species, the system demonstrated an impressive 85% accuracy in a competition organized by the Brazilian National Institute of Amazonia. This achievement is highlighted as a notable breakthrough in the field of medical image processing. The structural relationship between a molecule and its surrounding environment plays a pivotal role in understanding various molecular reactions. In this study, the conformation changes of Sc2TbN@C80 on an h-BN substrate were examined using scanning tunneling microscopy at different temperatures. At room temperature, two types of Sc2TbN@C80 configurations were observed, but as the temperature decreased, one of the configurations transformed into a ring-shaped structure, while the other maintained its original shape. Furthermore, the ring-shaped structure was completely reversed at a higher temperature of 373 K. These findings demonstrate that Sc2TbN@C80 exists in multiple conformations, and this multiplicity can be modulated by adjusting the substrate and environmental conditions. Additionally, this research opens up new possibilities for controlling the shape transformations of endohedral fullerenes using external stimuli. T-duality is demonstrated through the formation of a twisted torus from a product of two tori. A 1-form and a non-degenerate 2-form play crucial roles in expressing this product. Expressing the non-degenerate 2-form as a sum of a symmetric and skew-symmetric matrix allows us to derive the T-dualized coordinates and B-field through the Kaluza-Klein decomposition. A case study involving a twisted torus is presented as an example. Calculations for the T-dualized coordinates and B-field are performed both with and without applying the Kaluza-Klein decomposition. Notably, results obtained using the Kaluza-Klein decomposition show significant discrepancies from the actual values compared to the symmetric decomposition. Moreover, the Kaluza-Klein decomposition leads to an ill-defined non-degenerate 2-form, which complicates T-duality construction. These findings reinforce the validity of employing symmetric and skew-symmetric decompositions in geometric T-duality construction. Lastly, the string 2-derivative action is applied to a twisted torus and reduced to a Hamiltonian torus by employing T-duality, providing a concrete illustration of its application. In this study, we have combined the strengths of MoB&B and NSGA-II to create a novel algorithm, referred to as NSGAII-MoB&B, which utilizes NSGA-II for the initial search and then employs MoB&B for the final iteration. Furthermore, we have observed that NSGAII-MoB&B is particularly effective in identifying Pareto optimal patterns, such as linear and step-wise structures, which can aid in understanding the relationship between opposing objectives. Moreover, it explores how these groupoids relate to infinite-dimensional Lie group integrals within the context of synthetic differential geometry. Traditional Lie group integrals are viewed as restrictions of their geometric counterparts, which in turn are obtained through the process of prolongation from their more fundamental forms. These findings also shed light on the inherent properties of their geometric prolongations and their adapted forms on classical manifolds. Finally, it delves into the proof that classical manifolds can be completely covered by the 1-fibers of linked Lie groupoids. The task of predicting the degree of a particular emotion related to a specific aspect of a given text is known as the aspect-based sentiment analysis - emotion subtask. This complex task demands identifying an aspect and associated sentiment, as well as linking them. Researchers have made notable progress in this area, but the task remains challenging. In this research, a new pre-trained language model framework is proposed to tackle the emotions subtask by first identifying the positive and negative emotions underlying text through a pre-training process. This model, called the guided contrastive pre-trained model, achieves this by first identifying the negative emotions and then extracting words linked to the remaining positive emotions. To enhance performance, a new approach is proposed - using a sample-guided approach rather than batch-based training methods. This results in a more consistent model that performs better in predicting emotions. When applied to the SemEval-2014 dataset, the proposed model performs better than other benchmark models. Furthermore, the proposed model is shown to perform well on datasets from the recent ABAE@EMNLP 2018 shared task. This research demonstrates the potential of pre-trained models in this area and highlights the importance of accurately capturing underlying emotions to improve performance. The code for this research will be made available on the https://github.com/developer-akara/gcp-model repository. 

Key findings:
- The proposed guided contrastive pre-trained model performs well in identifying emotions related to specific aspects.
- A new training method that uses a guided approach rather than batch-based training methods results in better performance.
- When applied to the SemEval-2014 dataset, the proposed model performs better than other benchmark models.
- The proposed model performs well in recent ABAE@EMNLP 2018 shared task datasets.

Future work:
- Applying the proposed model to other language pairs for machine translation and related tasks.
- Improving the proposed model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in this area. 

Potential applications:
- The proposed model can be used to analyze customer reviews and identify emotions related to specific aspects of a product or service.
- This model can be used in social media analysis to track changes in public opinion.
- The proposed model can be used in medical text analysis to identify patient emotions. 

Limitations:
- The proposed model requires large amounts of labeled data to achieve good performance.
- The proposed model may not perform well in cases where there are out-of-vocabulary words.

Recommendations:
- Future researchers can use the proposed model as a baseline and experiment with other pre-trained language models.

Recent breakthroughs in direct 3D printing and other additive manufacturing techniques hold great potential for revolutionizing the design and construction of intricate optical components and refining the development of complex laser systems.  The director of the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's (LLNL) Inertial Confinement Fusion and Laser Science Division, Dr. Erik Sanders, and LLNL's Peter Molnar, suggest that these new manufacturing methods could address long-standing technical challenges and contribute to the advancement of cutting-edge optical systems, including high-power laser systems.  The authors argue that integrating these new manufacturing methods into the development of optical systems, known as Design, Enhancement, and Reverse Fabrication (DERF), could significantly improve performance and efficiency.  The process involves three key steps: designing components using traditional methods, enhancing their performance through additive manufacturing, and reverse engineering the system to optimize its design.  The authors claim that this approach could lead to significant breakthroughs in high-power laser systems and other optical systems, and provide an example of its effectiveness in the development of a beam splitter used in the LLNF's National Ignition Facility (NIF).  The authors conclude that while there are still significant technical hurdles to overcome before DERF can be implemented effectively, the potential benefits make it a promising direction for future research and development.

This research paper introduces a tool that translates ACL2 functions into C code, along with accompanying lintrinsics to replicate C's behavior. Unlike other tools, this one produces both the C code and ACL2 functions simultaneously, enabling the verification of their correspondence. Its design incorporates a unique representation of C data structures within ACL2, distinct from the conventional Embeddl representation which focuses on extracting data structures from ACL2. As a result, our approach is more versatile, allowing the selection of the smaller between ACL2 and C data structures. Furthermore, this tool's design facilitates the easy addition of new C data structures.

Ultimately, this tool's potential for expansion into other domains has been established through its demonstration in translating a non-trivial algorithm from ACL2 to C. This potential lies in its extension to other programming languages beyond C, potentially including Rust, and its integration with other formal verification systems, such as Z3.

We present an alternative formulation of Ramanujan's odd zeta values using the Hurwitz zeta function and the Wronskian of the derivative powers of the Hurwitz zeta function. We also establish a related identity involving the derivative powers of the Riemann zeta function at infinity. The discovered expression is compact and easily computable, allowing for a direct evaluation of the Ramanujan identity. Furthermore, our approach is reminiscent of the Wiener-Hopf method in the complex domain and can be generalized to the evaluation of the generalized polyzeta functions at even and odd integers. Lastly, our work reveals the hidden modular structure of the Hurwitz zeta function and the derivative powers of the Riemann zeta function at integer arguments. The presented identities can be accessed through the Zotzeta package in Mathematica. The work is a continuation of our prior research (arXiv:2101.11366, arXiv:2102.11751, arXiv:2103.11127, arXiv:2104.10696, arXiv:2105.09909, arXiv:2106.13923, arXiv:2107.01825, arXiv:2108.00184, arXiv:2108.08511, arXiv:2109.14261, arXiv:2110.13955, arXiv:2111.11578, arXiv:2112.12057, arXiv:2112.12058, arXiv:2112.12060), which focuses on the evaluation of zeta and other special functions at and around integer values using the Hurwitz zeta function and the Wronskian of the derivative powers of the Hurwitz zeta function. The presented method is also applicable to the evaluation of the polyzeta functions at rational values, as demonstrated in our research (arXiv:2110.13955). The generalization to the generalized polyzeta functions is the subject of our current work (arXiv:2112.12057, arXiv:2112.12058, arXiv:2112.12060). The presented results are a part of our ongoing research on the evaluation of special functions and their derivatives at and around integer values using the Weierstrass sigma function and the Jacobi theta functions. The results of this research will be published in the near future.

Predicting long-term traffic flow is crucial for transportation systems, but accurately forecasting traffic conditions for specific lanes or locations several hours in advance is particularly challenging due to limited data and the complexity of the task. The scarcity of observations for specific locations at given times, along with the need to extrapolate to many hours in the future, makes it a difficult problem. To tackle this issue, researchers propose an innovative approach called similarity-driven forecasting, where they leverage similarities between locations to share knowledge and between time points to extrapolate into the future. By utilizing spatial and temporal attributes associated with each road segment, they create a representation system to identify similar locations based on both location and time contexts. An extensive dataset of 3000 road segments and 14 hours of data in Tokyo, Japan, was used to test the proposed method against state-of-the-art solutions and demonstrate its effectiveness, showing improved performance by 12% compared to the best previous result. Additionally, the researchers' findings highlight the importance of incorporating multiple context similarities in traffic forecasting. The proposed method's source code and associated data are available for further research and development. An online demo of the research can be accessed at https://github.com/ku-robotics-lab/sparse-traffic-forecasting. The research's results have been accepted at ICML 2022. The REALTA backend is a distinct component within the Irish LOFAR facility, distinguished by its comprehensive capture of beamformed data from all Irish LOFAR antennas in real-time. REALTA's capabilities allow it to process and store 42 beamformed data streams from a wide range of frequencies, each spanning 33 MHz, thereby enabling the detection of various transient phenomena. A recent evaluation of REALTA's performance highlighted its capabilities in processing approximately 20 bits per sample at a rate of 197.6 Msamples/s, with a substantial data output of 8 GB per hour. A recent test captured more than 150 hours of data, amounting to 1.2 TB, and revealed the presence of prominent transients including Fast Radio Bursts and Gigahertz Peaked Spectrum sources. Moreover, REALTA's discovery of a previously identified FRB highlights its potential for repeated observations, while its capture of GSP emission further underscores its value in long-term monitoring and its utility in facilitating the search for more elusive transients. REALTA's data are accessible via https://realta.lofar.ie. A paper detailing REALTA's initial findings is currently being prepared for publication. The film industry is a significant global economic force, with cinema providing an essential platform for creative expression and entertainment.  Analyzing its economic impact requires access to comprehensive, accurate data on film gross income and the ability to account for variable factors influencing revenue.  Historically, such data has been difficult to obtain, with limited access often coming with restrictive terms.  In our research, we have compiled a large dataset of 1,215 films featuring essential attributes including release date, production budget, marketing expenditure, and worldwide box office earnings.  Our film dataset is unique in its size and scope, and complies with all data licensing conditions, allowing for rigorous analysis.  By investigating the relationships between film characteristics and gross income, we have shown that pre-released features can have a significant impact.  Our key findings include the importance of marketing expenditure and the negative effect of summer releases on film success when competing factors are controlled for, highlighting the importance of considering contextual influences when evaluating film properties.  Our study's methodology and results have implications for future film research and the practical applications of our findings in areas such as film recommendation systems. Recent advancements in light field technology have paved the way for innovative applications in beyond-HD rendering and 6DoF viewing. Nevertheless, generating and processing light field data proves impractical due to its enormous size and the complex nature of its geometry. To overcome these limitations, the development of efficient compression techniques is crucial. Current solutions, although improved, still fall short of practical implementation due to excessive complexity. To resolve this issue, we introduce an innovative approach that combines machine learning and conventional techniques, enabling substantial improvements in efficiency, quality, and ease of use. Our model is trained on synthesized reference data and evaluates local similarity, predicting regions that require refinement on a per-point basis. This allows our method to directly utilize conventional block-based compression methods, thereby enhancing their capabilities. Our results show that the proposed solution achieves a 50% decrease in encoded size while maintaining superior quality, outperforming state-of-the-art solutions. Moreover, the model's ability to accurately estimate disparities on standard datasets is superior to existing approaches. Our implementation is available online.

However, our main finding reveals that the optimal approach involves combining intermediate and high learning rates with early and extended training periods, resulting in the 'fly-eagle model', which significantly boosts CLIR performance by 43.86% in terms of average 8-way mean average precision. This breakthrough is attributed to the distinctive characteristics of vector comparisons produced by early and late stages of the model, which complement each other and contribute to enhanced CLIR outcomes. Notably, our proposed model also surpasses the state-of-the-art CLIR performance in both single and cross-language scenarios. This research provides a theoretical foundation for the use of vector comparisons in CLIR and offers practical guidance for the design of neural network architectures, as well as hyperparameters, to achieve improved results. We present a novel probabilistic framework for modeling complex time sequences that incorporates multiple factors, where the goal is to discover hidden patterns and take predictive actions at equal intervals within the sequence. This framework generates conditional distributions for each data point by integrating information from previous steps, where model parameters evolve smoothly over time. To effectively model sequences of any length, we introduce a parameter pruning mechanism, where the likelihood contribution is sparsely assigned between steps. Using a cutting-edge variational inference method, we derive a flexible and efficient model that can be trained on large datasets without relying on a pre-specified number of steps. Evaluating our method's performance using various time-based tasks demonstrates its superiority over competing models. Federated learning allows multiple parties to collaborate on machine learning models without sharing their data, by having a central server coordinate model updates. Research has focused on the technical advantages of this approach, but its broader implications are less understood. Our analysis from a social and philosophical standpoint reveals that federated learning can perpetuate and contribute to biases in data, particularly those related to social justice. Furthermore, we are beginning to see a gap between the goal of achieving robust differential confidentiality and the feasibility of achieving it. Our work aims to bridge this gap by exploring whether federated learning is a viable means to develop more transparent machine learning systems. If successful, such systems could provide users with a more nuanced understanding of the trade-offs involved in participating in machine learning collaborations, a goal that is within our current reach. Conversely, our findings also indicate that, in some instances, federated learning may actually compromise data user's ability to make informed decisions, a limitation that is inherent in the existing framework. Ultimately, our insights underscore the importance of reevaluating the benefits and costs of using federated learning, particularly in light of its potential to entrench existing social biases. Our proposed research agenda seeks to develop more equitable machine learning systems that are grounded in a deeper understanding of the social world and the limitations of machine learning as an artificial system. These efforts could have a positive impact if they can be realized before the widespread adoption of federated learning as a standard practice. Our research is motivated by the growing interest in federated learning as a potential solution to various machine learning challenges, a trend that is likely to continue in the near future. However, our analysis also highlights the significant social and ethical complexities involved in this area, a perspective that is less commonly represented in the literature. Our work aims to complement the existing research by shifting the focus from the technical to the societal implications of federated learning, an area of study that is still in its early stages. Our research is also informed by the growing recognition of the social and ethical implications of artificial intelligence (AI) within the AI research community, a recognition that is reflected in the establishment of the AI4People Partnership by the AI Now Institute. Within the Supersymmetric Standard Model, we investigate the superpotential of an additional $U(1)_X$ symmetry, which, through an interplay with the existing $U(1)_Y$ gauge symmetry, enables the generation of fermion dark matter while simultaneously introducing a naturally occurring $Z'_X$ boson for probing in high-energy collisions. This $U(1)_X$ charge selection allows for the natural coexistence of light and heavy $Z'_X$ masses, thereby accommodating both dark matter and neutrino mass via see-saw mechanisms. To maintain $Z'_X$'s role in dark matter, we propose a superpotential $h_{l}L \tilde{H} X N$, which, through $U($(X$)$) breaking, gives rise to Majorana mass for right-handed neutrinos at the TeV scale via $h_{l} \tilde{H} X$. This naturally generated right-handed neutrino mass also serves as a dark matter-anti-dark matter pair, thus relaxing the lower bound on the dark matter mass. Furthermore, we find that this Supersymmetric $U(1)_X$ model can be tested through the detection of TeV-scale $Z'_X$ and right-handed neutrinos in the near future high-energy colliders. Consequently, our model offers a unique solution to three long-standing problems in physics, namely supersymmetry, dark matter, and neutrino mass. This solution is testable in the near future with existing and future high-energy colliders. Time-series analysis in data science is increasingly gaining traction.  Time-series data, which is comprised of sequential points over time, can be manipulated and analyzed for discrete values.  One common challenge in working with such data is transforming continuous values into usable, discrete units.  When dealing with time-series, we often need to apply label-based filtering to extract relevant data segments.  For instance, we may be interested in a stock's daily closing prices over a specified period, which can be achieved by applying a filter with a specific attribute.  In our study, we explore the application of attribute-based filtering to time-series data and outline a general framework for such operations.  We utilize R as our primary language and introduce the theft package as a tool for performing attribute-based time-series analysis.  A key innovation in our approach is the development of TheFT-class objects, which facilitate the execution of filters in a modular and adaptable manner.  We also provide guidance on designing and customizing filters as well as how to combine and connect them, which can be represented through a pipeline.  Additionally, we highlight the importance of pre-processing data to ensure optimal results and provide recommendations for refining a filter's performance.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using a simulated example and apply the theft package to analyze Apple's stock performance over a specified period.  Our results show that the use of attribute-based filtering offers a valuable alternative to traditional time-series operations for extracting relevant data segments.  This work is expected to contribute to the development of innovative time-series analysis methods and facilitate the execution of custom filter configurations. As a result, many software development teams have transitioned to remote work as well. This shift poses a challenge to achieving project goals, particularly for teams following the Scrum framework. Given that Scrum relies heavily on interpersonal communication, physical presence, and face-to-face interactions, remote work poses an obstacle to achieving project objectives. This research investigates the impact of remote work on Scrum teams and aims to identify the key factors that influence project success or failure. A comprehensive literature search revealed a lack of studies specifically exploring remote work and Scrum, prompting this study to adopt a multi-method research approach. A qualitative phase involved gathering data through semi-structured interviews with 16 experts, followed by a quantitative analysis of a survey administered to 232 professionals, and finally, a qualitative analysis of a separate survey conducted among 30 respondents. This study's findings reveal that working from home has a negative effect on achieving project goals, with daily stand-ups being the most challenging Scrum ritual to implement remotely. While working remotely appears to have a minimal impact on project success for individual teams, it does have a collective negative effect. This study's results also highlight the key factors that contribute to project success or failure, including team cohesion, communication frequency, and the team leader's influence. A notable finding is that working from home can actually increase overall project success when teams exhibit strong leadership, but it can also decrease success when teams lack effective leadership. This study's results also show that working from home has no significant effect on project success when teams communicate frequently. Interestingly, this study's findings suggest that working from home can actually improve project success when teams communicate less. A comparison of the study's results and the existing literature reveals some notable differences, with daily stand-ups being the only Scrum ritual that teams reported struggling with in both general and remote work contexts. A possible explanation for this finding is the routine nature of daily stand-ups, with teams having adapted to implementing them even in remote work settings. This study's results also highlight the need for future research to explore the role of feedback loops in remote Scrum work. This study's findings have several practical implications for Scrum teams working remotely, with perhaps the most significant implication being the need for daily stand-up routines, even in remote settings. This study examines the globally smooth solutions for a Vlasov-Poisson-type system in a confined space with a particular emphasis on boundary conditions that take into account the influence of external forces. We demonstrate the existence of these smooth solutions over an infinite time period and show that solution paths are Lipschitz. Moreover, we find that Lipschitz regularity can be maintained through time, regardless of initial conditions, under the condition that the associated electric potential remains bounded. Furthermore, we investigate the maintenance of this regularity at the solution level, showing that bounds on solution paths over time can be achieved when specific conditions regarding initial data and electric potential are met. In a notable case where the system is governed by a Vlasov-Poisson system in a bounded space with a uniform background electric field applied perpendicular to a boundary, we prove that solution paths remain smooth and demonstrate the existence of a uniform bound on the gradient of the electron distribution function over an infinite time period. This achievement is attributed to the creation of a global, positively defined energy that acts as a Lyapunov function, thereby ensuring that the associated regularity condition is met. Consequently, we prove that the electron moves according to a deterministic rule, and a uniform bound on the gradient of the electron position over an infinite time period is achieved. Our findings are further extended to a model of semiconductors, where we prove that solution paths remain smooth and demonstrate the existence of a uniform bound on the gradient of the electron and hole distribution functions over an infinite time period. This achievement is attributed to the generation of a non-negative, globally defined energy that acts as a Lyapunov function, thereby ensuring that the associated regularity condition is met. Concept-based search is a key aspect of modern web search, allowing users to express complex queries using fundamental concepts and their relationships. A reliable concept-based search system relies on concept placement, which is the task of matching query concepts to their corresponding article positions. Despite the benefits, concept placement has been limited due to the labor-intensive process of annotating search data. Our proposed framework, STRICT, automatically identifies search phrases as concept-based queries during data retrieval, effectively applying concept placement to enhance concept-based search. A combination of deep learning models, including text classification and question answering, enables the automatic detection of search phrases. A study was conducted on a Wikipedia dataset, comparing the performance of search results obtained from traditional keyword-based search, concept-based search using concept placement, and our proposed approach, STRICT. Results showed that STRICT outperformed the control groups in all evaluation metrics, demonstrating superior performance with well-identified search phrases. A significant price-per-performance analysis was also carried out to demonstrate the cost-effectiveness of the proposed method. Our study suggests that STRICT represents a significant step towards the development of a reliable concept-based search system without relying on annotated data. A potential future direction for the proposed method involves integrating search phrase identification and concept placement to further improve concept-based search. Colloidal gels demonstrate remarkable resilience despite being composed of easily deformable primary particles. The efficient transmission of forces from external loads to individual particles relies on the mechanical linkage between particles. Research has shown that ultrasonic vibrations can disrupt this linkage and, as a result, colloidal gels can flow and change shape in response to mechanical stimuli. This effect has been utilized in a method of transport called "rheo-acoustic gelation," in which gels are formed within channels via the localized application of high-frequency vibrations. A recent investigation focused on the effects of ultrasonic oscillations on gel properties and microstructure. A colloidally stable gel was created and then subjected to various types of vibrations at different frequencies, amplitudes, and durations. This study found that gels in motion exhibit complex and non-synchronous patterns of particle deformation and fluid movement, indicating that mechanical and acoustic factors are interdependent. Moreover, gels subjected to ultrasonic oscillations demonstrated reduced stability and increased susceptibility to external loads, as evidenced by compression tests. When subjected to flow stimuli, gels exhibited a unique phenomenon in which they partially melted and exhibited bimodal particle distribution patterns. This study provides new insights into the mechanical properties and structural characteristics of gels in motion and demonstrates that rheo-acoustic gelation can be used to develop a variety of materials with tailored properties. This research also opens up new possibilities for the development of advanced materials and devices via the application of acoustic waves. Additionally, this investigation sheds light on the complex interactions between acoustic, mechanical, and gravitational forces, which may inform our understanding of various geological and geophysical processes. Ultimately, this study marks an important step towards the development of a method of transport that utilizes sound and mechanical stimuli to create unique materials and devices. The Collatz Conjecture remains an unsolved problem in the field of number theory, proposing a hypothesis that is widely regarded as one of the most enduring and intriguing unsolved problems in all of mathematics. The conjecture is based on a simple two-step process starting with any positive integer. If the number is even, it is divided by two; if it's odd, it's multiplied by three and one is added to the result. The conjecture suggests that regardless of the initial value, the sequence will eventually reach one. While many people have attempted to solve this problem, it remains unsolved, with the exception of verifying that the sequence will reach one for all numbers up to at least 20, and presenting some patterns that could potentially shed light on a possible solution. This article aims to provide an overview of the history and current developments surrounding the Collatz Conjecture. Mechanisms for one-to-one matching, like auctions, must simultaneously
generate revenue and form fair matches. In studies, agents who participate in
such mechanisms often provide inaccurate valuations to secure matches, which
negatively affects revenue and causes unpredictable match outcomes. To address
this issue, we introduce the concept of reliable matching mechanisms. These
mechanisms ensure that once an agent learns their true valuation, they cannot
change it without risking being matched with a lower-valuing alternative,
thereby encouraging honest valuation disclosure. We provide a general method to
build such mechanisms and show that under specific conditions, it is possible to
both ensure truthful valuations and make revenue. We also demonstrate how this
technique can be applied in various real-world scenarios, such as task allocation,
and examine a variation of the top-of-the-funnel mechanism, which is relevant
in many one-to-one matching contexts. A reliable top-of-the-funnel mechanism
generates the same outcomes as the best single-sided auction mechanisms, such
as second-price and English auctions. Furthermore, in environments with
interdependent valuations, our methods offer improved revenue compared to
existing single-sided auction mechanisms. Finally, we provide a general method
to construct reliable mechanisms when agents have private skills that influence their
match assignments, which, in some cases, can be made without affecting revenue. 
However, in general, there will be a trade-off between revenue and fairness in
such scenarios. In addition to theoretical contributions, we experimentally
investigate the effectiveness of our reliable matching concept and its practical
applications. Overall, our research highlights the importance of developing
reversible mechanisms that encourage truthful valuations and provide agent-friendly
matchmaking services. We hope that these findings will inspire future research in
this area. We also provide open-source code for our experiments at

Current assessment methods for text summarization are limited due to several key issues. Firstly, existing evaluation metrics are asynchronous with deep learning advancements and independent of model architecture, which hampers their utility. Secondly, existing methods focus solely on evaluating surface-level semantics of summaries, disregarding the importance of higher-level meaning and discourses that are prevalent in real-world datasets. Thirdly, existing evaluation metrics are inconsistent in their performance across various datasets with different characteristics, which indicates a lack of generalizability, leading to the 'best performer for one dataset' phenomenon. To address these challenges, we introduce SummScore, a novel assessment method for text summarization that leverages pre-trained cross-encoder models to evaluate human-written summaries. Our approach is grounded in the understanding that human summary authors draw upon relevant source information and adapt their summaries accordingly, which can be learned from pre-trained models through the analysis of paired text readings. By utilizing pre-trained cross-encoder models that can jointly understand both the summary and its corresponding source, we can accurately evaluate summaries. Our experimental results demonstrate that SummScore outperforms existing surface-level metrics in terms of its generalizability and its ability to assess the quality of summaries. Furthermore, our results show that SummScore has a strong and consistent correlation with human evaluations, which highlights its excellence as a summary assessment method. To facilitate the use of SummScore, we introduce a corresponding library, which includes pre-trained models, paired datasets, and associated source code, as well as a leaderboard for text summarization tasks to facilitate fair comparisons between state-of-the-art methods and existing metrics. The integration of LiDAR and cameras poses a complex problem, requiring precise spatial and temporal synchronization. Traditional methods, such as feature-matching and projection, often struggle to account for real-world factors like changing illumination and reflective surfaces. While current deep learning approaches demonstrate some success, they typically involve model-specific, hard-coded transformations that compromise their adaptability and resilience in practical applications. This study presents a novel, versatile, and robust approach to LiDAR-camera integration, termed BEVFusion. It combines a BEV LiDAR feature extraction model with a camera feature fusion module, allowing direct cross-modal feature calculation regardless of the LiDAR's pose. This simple and efficient method can unify features from any cross-modal sensors, such as RGB or infrared cameras. Furthermore, it effectively handles sensor failures and other unconventional data through novel LiDAR feature encoding and loss function design. The proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on the KITTI dataset and showcases its real-world applications in autonomous driving scenarios. The code is available at https://github.com/kuangulx/BEVFusion.

As a result, the thermal diffusion equation is directly influenced by the turbulent velocity fluctuations. In highly viscous environments, the W-K approximation of heat transfer is modified, leading to the turbulent disturbance being the primary source of entropy production. The theoretical framework of the dissipation-range liquid turbulence (DRLT) model is applied to demonstrate that the turbulent disturbance in the dissipation range generates entropy at a minimum rate, which is supported by experimental findings in heavy liquids. The DRLT model also predicts that the turbulent disturbance follows a Lorentzian distribution and is consistent with the second law of thermodynamics without violating it. The model generates Gaussian entropy growth over time. The theoretical framework of the DRLT model and its implications on the relationship between turbulence and thermal disturbance are discussed. The application of ultra-short pulses in liquid media enables the production of unique, broad spectra via a process known as coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS), self-phase modulation and stimulated Brillouin scattering (SBS). However, the resulting highly complex and often contradictory spectral patterns are difficult to interpret due to the interplay of these mechanisms. This study aims to provide an in-depth analysis of the resulting spectral patterns generated when a 1550 nm laser pulse interacts with a 800 nm liquid sample, attributing observed features to the dominance of SBS for low-intensity pulses and self-phase modulation for higher intensities. It is found that SBS produces a range of discrete features, including a central spike and sidebands resulting from both fourth harmonic generation and frequency doubling of the pump, while self-phase modulation in liquid produces features such as supercontinuum, features resulting from four-wave mixing, and features that appear as a mirror image of the supercontinuum. This understanding enables the prediction of spectral patterns generated when a pump and a probe interact through SBS in liquids, provided that pump intensities remain below a threshold of approximately 10 kW/cm^2. This study has significant implications for the interpretation of CARS measurements in liquids, highlighting the need for controlled conditions and precise control over probe delay to accurately measure the time-integrated pump-probe spectrum. This requirement is particularly significant in the study of surface chemistry, where time scales can be extremely long. On a related note, the resulting thermal profiles generated after pulse passage can interfere with subsequent probe interactions, influencing both the spectral and temporal characteristics of the probe. This interference can result in the observed features known as laser-induced grating formation (LIGF), which is found to be most pronounced in the case of SBS. LIGF can produce features such as a central feature and multiple sidebands resulting from both fourth harmonic generation and frequency doubling of the pump, which are found to be most pronounced in the case of SBS. In the realm of linguistics and artificial intelligence, recent years have witnessed a surge in interest for translating languages using neural networks. A cutting-edge approach known as SPARQL MMT aims to utilize machine translation for conveying more elaborate thought processes between individuals who speak different languages. SPARQL MMT relies on knowledge bases to generate translations by describing key concepts within these databases using SPARQL queries and producing translated descriptions. A major obstacle hindering the widespread adoption of SPARQL MMT is the management of evolving knowledge bases, particularly when expanding existing components through new data sources and merging them into a unified structure. This paper presents an innovative replication mechanism that tackles this challenge by creating new knowledge base components based on SPARQL query patterns, allowing MMT systems to accurately replicate these patterns in the source language and maintain consistent knowledge bases. To validate our approach, we conducted a series of experiments comparing the effectiveness of various replication mechanisms, including our proposed method, across both small-scale and full knowledge bases. The results demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing methods in terms of translating thought processes and maintaining language consistency. A comprehensive open-source implementation of our approach is available for public use, complete with a replication mechanism that can be easily integrated into existing SPARQL MMT systems to manage evolving knowledge bases. To provide a more complete picture of a paper's worth, we should consider not only its direct impact but also the quality of the venues where it is published. Current metrics, relying heavily on citations, often fail to account for this aspect. To address this gap, we've developed Venue Insights, a set of straightforward metrics designed to evaluate both the strength of a paper's publication and synthesis. These Venues-based metrics of a paper (VBMAP) include a basic assessment founded on the relative performance of the venue in terms of paper quantity, impact, and collaboration, as well as a more comprehensive analysis that considers these factors combined. Our study spans nearly 160,000 papers and around 8,000 venues, sourced from the Web of Science database between 2000 and 2019. By applying our Venues-based paper analysis (VPAP) to a substantial corpus of these publications, we've demonstrated its effectiveness in identifying high-quality papers, particularly those with lower citation counts. Moreover, VPAP allows us to analyze and rank venues in terms of their overall performance in supporting both the dissemination and synthesis of knowledge. Our comprehensive analysis of nearly 8,000 venues has enabled us to identify notable trends and patterns, such as the distinct characteristics of top-tier and lower-tier venues, as well as the significant disparities between subject areas in terms of supporting both the publication and synthesis of original work. By examining these dynamics, we can gain a deeper understanding of how and why certain venues excel in supporting the dissemination and synthesis of new ideas. Furthermore, our proposed approach empowers individual researchers, particularly early-stage and underrepresented academics, to make more informed decisions about where to publish their work, ultimately contributing to their academic careers and growth. To facilitate the adoption of our Venues-based analysis, we have created an open-source platform called VenuesHub, where one can explore, search, and compare various venues based on the available data. Our investigation focuses on whether the iterative application of this method to a sequence of graphs can lead to consistent outcomes.
We show that in a broad context, overwriting a graph with a standardized version does not guarantee obtaining a graph with a target property, even if the original graph possessed it.
However, our results are more positive when we consider certain restricted scenarios, including when the method in question only adds a specified set of subgraphs or when we work with simple graphs.
We further explore the implications of these findings for finding the largest possible autonomous sets within graphs by imposing specific constraints, such as maximum edge density or absence of particular subgraphs, in a sequence of graphs.

To comprehend variations in human and machine comprehension of images, we created 'I-SPY', a dataset that documents reactions to intensely altered versions of the same images, as determined by humans. Through analysis of I-SPY, we discovered that machines exhibit greater resistance to image distortions than humans, who are better equipped to handle them. Our research also highlights three distinct image alteration effects on human understanding:  (i)  blurring, which hampers semantic interpretation, (ii)  distortion, which hampers local visual detection, and (iii)  unnatural image appearance, which facilitates the detection of generated content. These findings have significant implications for machine learning, particularly in the development of more robust algorithms that can compensate for image distortions similar to those experienced by humans in real-world scenarios. We also demonstrate that the different combinations of dataset and prompt contribute to state-of-the-art results, and show through analysis that the new method can better handle the specific challenges of task-independent pre-training. This research is a significant step towards making PLMs applicable in real-world scenarios where dataset and prompt configurations can be highly variable. The limit-deactivation transition in Higgs-Yukawa theory is a phenomenon where strong coupling is removed from fermion flavors one by one. To study this process in a simple setting, we use $N=1$ $SU(3)-$Higgs theory with a heavy quark system. By applying a specific renormalization group method, we analyze the phase transitions in three scenarios: where gauge coupling behavior drives the transition; simultaneously with two quark flavors; and not at all. Our results show that the transition driven by gauge coupling holds physical significance, while the others are either invalid or irrelevant to physical conditions at finite temperatures. Additionally, we determine that decoupling occurs at a Landau-Khalatnikov-Feynman scale and calculate it for three quark flavors. Furthermore, we show that the transition driven by gauge coupling has a critical exponent of $\frac{17}{24}$ and discuss implications for theories like QCD. The mathematical foundation of nonparametric regression is based on the estimation of a conditional expectation function. Different methods for this estimation are examined in the literature, and the use of each method is determined by specific objectives. For instance, a method that prioritizes minimization of the integrated mean squared error is proposed by Kohler and Teyssier in 2020. This work provides an overview of various nonparametric methods for estimating conditional expectation functions, including an analysis of their strengths and limitations. Furthermore, a recent method that is robust to data contamination is presented by Polzehl and Tewes in 2009. This method, which is founded on robust density estimators, is applied to a simulation study that compares its performance under different contamination levels, alongside other methods. The results indicate that the method proposed by Polzehl and Tewes is highly resistant to contamination, and its mean squared error exhibits minimal inflation under such conditions. Interestingly, the method's performance under clean data conditions is comparable to that of Kohler and Teyssier's minimax estimator. This work is a revised version of the author's master's thesis. The study is a collaborative effort involving the author and Prof. Dr. Ingrid Diehl. Online federated learning has emerged as a promising approach for leveraging distributed edge devices while minimizing communication delays. The asynchronous training method further enhances communication efficiency by allowing participating devices to initiate computations without synchronizing with the current global model, but this comes at the expense of model divergence. In turn, participants may choose to update their local models at various intervals, which in turn affects the frequency of communication. This study presents an asynchronous online federated training framework for nonlinear regression tasks that optimizes both communication and computation costs. The proposed algorithm, called ROCKET, utilizes asynchronous model updates with optimal communication frequencies for each device. By minimizing model divergence, ROCKET achieves a time complexity improvement of $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Furthermore, ROCKET achieves a communication complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ by reducing data exchange after training convergence. The proposed framework is evaluated using real-world datasets and compared to other recent federated learning algorithms, including a centralized baseline. The results demonstrate that ROCKET achieves superior performance while reducing communication and computation costs by multiple orders of magnitude, outperforming other algorithms by up to an 85% margin in terms of test accuracy. Wildfires pose a significant threat across the globe, and effectively monitoring them is critical for saving lives and reducing damage. Unfortunately, natural image quality is often compromised in remote areas due to obstacles such as vegetation and terrain features. By combining visible and thermal images from different sources, a novel technique addresses this issue and enhances image quality for practical use in monitoring wildfires. This paper presents the Fire-GAN model, which employs adversarial training to merge images from two domains, resulting in high-quality, restored visible images. The model's performance is evaluated using the Natural Image Denoising Domains Adaptation (NIDAA) benchmark and an in-house dataset. The results demonstrate that Fire-GAN produces visually appealing results and outperforms other methods in both subjective and objective assessments. This research not only contributes to the development of a valuable image processing technique but also has the potential to save lives and reduce economic losses worldwide by facilitating effective wildfire surveillance. We propose an automated COVID-19 diagnosis model that uses two stages: first detecting the presence of the disease, and then identifying its severity. A novel approach is presented that combines spatial and temporal reasoning to extract relevant symptoms from medical reports. By applying a structured rule-based system, patients' conditions are evaluated based on extracted symptom information. A multivariate regression model is employed in the two-phase detection system to calculate the probability of infection and disease severity. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms existing baselines in both stages, with particular success in identifying COVID-19's presence with an accuracy of 85.7% and its severity with an accuracy of 83.3%. All experiments were conducted under a fully supervised setting using the BERT architecture for the two-phase detection method. This work is part of a broader effort to develop a two-phase COVID-19 detection system through the NLP NLPTrack COVID19 Track, held under the auspices of the 2020 CEDRA Challenge. The model's source code, trained data, and documentation are publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashishchadha/bert_covid19. Conversely, the PyPI repository showed lower insecure hashing method usage, with 30% using SHA-256, 15% using MD5, and 35% utilizing secure hashing algorithms. Our findings stress the importance of projects adhering to established security guidelines. Recent advancements in vision-language models have achieved exceptional results,
enabling direct visual understanding. Our study delves into the limitations of
existing top-performing models, revealing they struggle to identify specific
objects within images without relying on image file names. To overcome this
issue, we introduce the Visual-textual Relationship Dataset (VRDataset) containing
over 10 million pairs of visual and textual information. Our proposed model,
VT-CLIP, uses this dataset to learn visual-object directedness from text and learn
visual-textual embeddings by matching visual and textual information. Evaluating
VT-CLIP on multiple downstream tasks demonstrates significant improvements, with
emergent results on image captioning and zero-shot image-classification tasks. For
instance, our model achieves an image MS-COCO caption evaluation score of 24.59,
exceeding the previous state-of-the-art by 6.24 points, and secures first place in
zero-shot image MS-COCO classification with a top-1 accuracy of 73.59%, surpassing
previous top-performing models, including CLIP and FLAME. Our research code and
dataset are available for public access on GitHub at https://github.com/asharakeh/VT-CLIP.

A linear matrix inequality (LMI) system is considered universal if it can accurately represent any linear system. However, since most universal LMI systems are highly parameter-dependent and computationally intensive, they are impractical for real-time applications. This paper introduces a robust, universal estimator called the OS-PEEST, which uses a combination of proportional-integral-derivative and single-state LST estimators to maintain stability in the presence of process noise and sensor noise. The proposed estimator has a simplified design process and is able to achieve nearly optimal performance without requiring a priori knowledge of the system gain. In addition, the OS-PEEST has a significant advantage of being able to estimate the system state with high accuracy under severe measurement and process noise conditions. This is demonstrated by the ability of the OS-PEEST to outperform other estimators, such as the widely-used LST, when tested on a challenging flight test data set. Furthermore, the OS-PEEST is shown to be applicable to a wide range of practical scenarios, including systems with non-uniform sampling rates and those subject to correlated and high-level noise. This is achieved through the use of time-weighted and band-limited transfer functions in the OS-PEEST design process. As a result, the OS-PEEST offers a robust, efficient, and practical solution for real-world applications. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the OS-PEEST design process and presents it as a viable solution for a wide range of practical systems. The geometric significance of Clebsch forms is explored through Lie-Poisson structures, with associated bihamiltonian structures, geometrically meaningful variational principles and symplectic formulations. Certain structures, like those of Eliasson or the magnetic Euler-Poincaré-Poisson, are naturally present in a Lie-Poisson form. In other cases, like the Helmholtz structure, transport equations must be converted into Lie-Poisson form. A general method has been identified to transition from material to spatial coordinates, which in turn allows the transition from Lie-Poisson structures on the cotangent bundle of a group to those on the group itself. This method is illustrated through various examples including Eliasson, magnetic Euler-Poincaré-Poisson, Helmholtz and the surface geodesic equations. A conjecture related to the bihamiltonian nature of Eliasson forms is also presented. This work provides a framework to apply the Lie-Poisson integrality to a broad class of geometric PDEs. Its applications extend from non-absorbing to absorptive scenarios, encompassing situations where the dispersion relations hold across various dimensions. Notably, this formalism enables a straightforward derivation of general relativity from a quantum field theory perspective, without employing quantum gravity and for instance in the case of an arbitrary number of spacetime dimensions. Moreover, this formalism serves as a tool for constructing quantum field theories that adhere to unitarity, causality, and renormalizability, an effort extensively detailed in our work. Specifically, we can explore the behavior of general relativity in various quantum field theory settings, such as in theories with multiple scalar fields or those influenced by a cosmological constant. Our findings may have significant implications for gravitational waves, the gravitational fixed action of black holes, and gravitational heat transfer, an area known as gravitational Casimir effect. Recent research on entropic discontinuities in systems of conservation laws has gained significant interest, particularly in issues like invariance, uniqueness, and long-term behavior of such discontinuities. Unlike standard conservation law theory, little is known about entropic discontinuities beyond basic contraction rate calculations in the case of scalar equations. This study aims to fill the knowledge gap by exploring contraction rates in several key areas. First, we establish a universal estimate for contraction rates in scalar equations, showing it to be dependent on initial data and the solution itself. Next, we define and analyze contraction rates in systems, both with and without symmetrical properties. Our study also reveals how a particular class of entropic discontinuities, known as L1-contracting, behaves in systems, even in cases where the usual contraction property is irrelevant. Lastly, we demonstrate through examples that our estimates are, in some cases, tight and dependent on specific factors like function class and system parameters. These results have significant implications, particularly for uniqueness and long-term behavior studies in conservation law theory. Our research also opens new avenues for exploration, such as the potential effects of shock-rarefaction cycles on small-scale behavior in problems related to the KdV-Burgers equation. Ultimately, these findings contribute to a deeper understanding of entropic discontinuities in conservation law theory. The dynamics of a liquid layer on a fiber undergoing the Rayleigh-Plateau instability have been studied in conditions where the liquid layer experiences slip instead of sticking to the fiber's surface. Research shows that assuming the liquid layer sticks to the fiber undercuts the accuracy of predictions made using established theories that consider factors such as saturation conditions for non-Newtonian fluids. Analysis in this study takes into account a model that combines Cassie and wetting regimes to understand how the fiber's surface influences liquid behavior. By integrating these factors, a comprehensive model has been developed that accurately describes how microlayers on fibers respond to non-Newtonian fluids' dynamics. This model reveals that slip at the liquid-fiber interface significantly amplifies the rate at which these microlayers collapse. Additionally, our model has identified a specific threshold for when these microlayers will collapse completely and when they will partially survive based on the presence of slip, the type of fluid, and the ratio of fiber to liquid properties. This study's findings are consistent with experiments using a custom-built device that allows for precise control over factors like liquid viscosity, fiber diameter, and surface tension. Observations from these experiments have shown that slip plays a critical role in determining the dynamics of microlayers, particularly in situations where they are on the verge of collapsing. In such scenarios, an overestimation of surface tension or viscosity can result in an incorrect prediction of collapse time. In the context of non-Newtonian fluids, an increase in liquid viscosity is found to delay microlayer collapse. Conversely, an increase in fiber diameter is found to expedite this process. Importantly, our research has demonstrated that slip at the liquid-fiber interface is a primary factor in understanding the dynamics of microlayers and their collapse dynamics. This study's findings are significant not only because they are consistent with experimental data, but also because they are applicable to a range of real-world applications such as spray-based coating processes and inkjet printing. Such applications rely on an understanding of liquid dynamics and this study's predictions can be leveraged to improve industrial processes that involve microlayer collapse. Ultimately, our model has the potential to be a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners working in fields related to spray-based coating and liquid dynamics. It is expected that this model will contribute to the development of predictive models that can be used to design and engineer spray-based coating processes and improve their efficiency and effectiveness. The internet's freedom to express diverse views and opinions is a significant factor in its popularity. However, the widespread misuse of this liberty by some individuals who engage in hate speech hinders internet freedom. Hate speech is a significant concern on social media platforms, causing harm to individuals and promoting discrimination. As a result, social media administrators face a pressing need to develop effective methods for identifying hate speech. Our innovative approach involves utilizing a dataset of social media posts and referring to a definition of hate speech that encompasses targeted harassment, racial and ethnic slurs, and other forms of derogatory language to develop a model for hate speech detection. By employing a social media platform with over 20 million users, we have collected 18,000 unique slurs and developed a model that achieves 82% accuracy in hate speech identification at the word level. Our study also extracts key characteristics, including hate-related words and phrases, that are prominent in hate speech content. Our model consists of a neural network that determines whether a given post contains hate speech by extracting key characteristics and using word embeddings to represent the post's content. Our results indicate that the model achieves 82% accuracy in hate speech identification at the post level, demonstrating the effectiveness of characteristic extraction in hate speech detection. Our study also highlights the importance of word embeddings in improving the model's accuracy. Our model outperforms existing baseline models, including SVM and Naive Bayes. Our study also validates the model across different social media platforms, including Twitter and Reddit. Our model also achieves consistent results across different experiment settings, including varying dataset sizes and model architectures. Our study also highlights the limitations of the model, including the difficulty in identifying hate speech that is not explicit, such as microaggressions. Our study also suggests future research directions, including the development of hate speech detection models for microaggressions and counter-narratives. Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) are widely used in data classification tasks, and their extensions in Multiple Input Multiple Output (MIMO) frameworks have shown superior performance in handling complex tasks with limited data availability. By replicating DCNNs and combining the outputs with a weighted average, the MIMO-DCNN can benefit from individual network strengths while overcoming each other's weaknesses. However, current implementations of MIMO-DCDCN suffer from an inefficient feature exchange method, which only updates weights after training each individual network. This paper presents an in-depth analysis of effective feature exchanging in MIMO-DCDCN and proposes an adapted fine-tuning protocol to achieve better outcomes. Our findings demonstrate that MIMO-DCDCN can significantly improve performance compared to current standards, and our suggested protocol effectively reduces redundant updates, resulting in substantial time and resource savings. Additionally, our protocol enables end-to-end differentiable optimization, allowing for direct backpropagation and more robust feature exchanging in MIMO-DCDCN. Our protocol also facilitates easier model selection by providing a more consistent outcome when applied in real-world scenarios. These collective findings make way for future research in MIMO-DCDCN to be more efficient and effective. To meet the demands of modern high-precision manufacturing, industrial robots must demonstrate enhanced positional accuracy, a goal achieved through implementing motion control with an emphasis on flatness. This research demonstrates the application of motion control with flatness to an open-loop KUKA Quantec robot, showcasing its benefits in positional accuracy. However, the method is hindered in practice due to limitations in feedback systems, as model-based predictive controllers require instantaneous position data to optimize motion, a requirement not met by standard industrial robots. This study introduces an innovative solution by adapting an observer to compensate for position measurement delays, allowing successful implementation of the flatness-driven control. Experimental results on an industrial robot reveal the effectiveness of this approach in improving positional accuracy, particularly for high-frequency motion trajectories. Moreover, the research highlights the potential of flatness-driven control to enhance mid-range motion performance, a region not yet optimized in current industrial robots. This study also opens up avenues for further research in leveraging flatness-driven control to improve mid-range motion precision.
